title: Dates, times, and durations
goal: Parse dates explicitly and use calendar-aware operations.
prerequisites: You can convert types and select rows by conditions.

cells.title: Turn date text into dates
cells.explanation: A date-looking string is still text until it is parsed. `to_datetime()` converts it to a date/time type. An explicit format removes ambiguity; impossible dates can be marked as NaT, pandas missing date value.
cells.code:
source = pd.Series(["2026-09-01", "2026-09-03", "2026-02-30"], dtype="string")
result = pd.to_datetime(source, format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
print(result)
print("Unparsed dates:", result.isna().sum())

questions.answer: Four-digit year, numeric month, and day of month.
It becomes NaT because it is not a valid calendar date.

questions.prompt: Why might 01/02/2026 be ambiguous without a format?
questions.answer: It could mean January 2 or February 1, depending on the intended date convention.

cells.task: Parse ["01/09/2026", "03/09/2026", "30/02/2026"] as day/month/year. Count invalid dates.
cells.solution:
source = pd.Series(["01/09/2026", "03/09/2026", "30/02/2026"], dtype="string")
result = pd.to_datetime(source, format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce")
print(result)
print("Unparsed dates:", result.isna().sum())
cells.solution_note: The first two dates are September 1 and September 3. February 30 remains invalid.

check.feedback: NaT marks a missing or unparseable date/time value.

cells.solution_verify:
assert result.iloc[0] == pd.Timestamp("2026-09-01")
assert result.iloc[1].day == 3
assert result.isna().sum() == 1
cells.watch: Inspect parsing failures; errors="coerce" does not repair the source date.

cells.title: Extract useful calendar parts
cells.explanation: After parsing dates, the `.dt` accessor exposes calendar parts such as year, month, and weekday. These features are useful for grouping and checking patterns. Do not try to use `.dt` on unparsed strings.
cells.code:
df = students()
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df[["Student_ID", "Join_Date"]].copy()
result["Month"] = result["Join_Date"].dt.month
result["Weekday"] = result["Join_Date"].dt.day_name()
print(result.head(4))

questions.prompt: Why can .dt be used on Join_Date here?
questions.answer: The column has been converted from text into a datetime type.

questions.prompt: Will all Month values be the same in this dataset?
questions.answer: Yes, all join dates are in September, so every Month is 9.

questions.prompt: Why might a month number need a year too in a larger dataset?
questions.answer: September from different years would otherwise be grouped together.

cells.task: Add Year and Day columns for the same join dates. Store only the first three rows in result, with columns Student_ID, Year, Month, and Day, then print result.
cells.solution:
df = students()
dates = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": df["Student_ID"], "Year": dates.dt.year, "Month": dates.dt.month, "Day": dates.dt.day}).head(3)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The years are 2026, the months are 9, and the day values are 1, 2, and 3.
cells.watch: A weekday pattern in twelve fictional records is a practice result, not evidence about real student behavior.
cells.takeaway: Create date features after parsing the date type.

cells.title: Filter an explicit date interval
cells.explanation: Date comparisons let you select a time interval. `between()` includes both boundaries by default; naming the inclusive rule makes your intent clearer. Here every date is a midnight date with no separate time-of-day information.
cells.code:
df = students()
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
mask = df["Join_Date"].between("2026-09-03", "2026-09-06", inclusive="both")
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Join_Date"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why do interval boundary rules matter?
questions.answer: An included or excluded endpoint changes which records contribute to the analysis.

cells.task: Select dates on or after September 3 and strictly before September 6 using two comparisons.
cells.solution:
df = students()
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
mask = (df["Join_Date"] >= "2026-09-03") & (df["Join_Date"] < "2026-09-06")
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Join_Date"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S003, S004, and S005 remain. The exclusive upper boundary removes S006.

check.prompt: Which operator excludes the upper boundary?
check.feedback: A strict less-than comparison excludes an equal endpoint.

cells.watch: With timestamps containing hours, an end date at midnight is not the whole final day; a next-day exclusive bound is often clearer.
cells.takeaway: State the start and end rules of every date filter.

cells.title: Calculate elapsed time with a fixed reference
cells.explanation: Subtracting dates produces timedeltas, which represent durations. `.dt.days` extracts whole days from those durations. A fixed reference date makes a classroom result reproducible when the file is opened later.
cells.code:
df = students()
joined = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
reference = pd.Timestamp("2026-10-01")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": df["Student_ID"], "Days_enrolled": (reference - joined).dt.days})
print(result.head(4))

questions.prompt: What object is produced by reference - joined?
questions.answer: A Series of time durations, called timedeltas.

questions.prompt: How many elapsed days does S001 have on October 1?
Why use a fixed reference instead of today()?
questions.answer: Everyone can reproduce the same answer, regardless of when they run the lesson.

cells.task: Change the reference to October 8 and select students with at least 30 elapsed days enrolled.
cells.hint: Recalculate the duration, then filter Days_enrolled >= 30.
cells.solution:
df = students()
joined = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
reference = pd.Timestamp("2026-10-08")
df["Days_enrolled"] = (reference - joined).dt.days
result = df.loc[df["Days_enrolled"] >= 30, ["Student_ID", "Days_enrolled"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S001 through S008 meet the rule. S008 has exactly 30 elapsed days.

check.prompt: Does elapsed time count both the start and end date as full extra days?
options: No; it is the duration between the two dates
check.feedback: Date subtraction measures elapsed time. Inclusive calendar-day counts are a separate reporting rule.

cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 8
assert result.iloc[-1]["Student_ID"] == "S008"
assert result.iloc[-1]["Days_enrolled"] == 30
cells.watch: For real timestamps, keep time zones consistent before subtracting them.
cells.takeaway: Use timedelta arithmetic instead of subtracting date strings.
